content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published recommendations in 2018 regarding non-clinical interventions aimed at reducing unnecessary cesarean sections. These recommendations include various educational and supportive strategies targeted at pregnant women, their partners, and healthcare professionals. Below is a detailed explanation of the interventions described: 1. Antenatal Education Programs: Masoumi et al. (2016): A childbirth preparation program was conducted in eight sessions, each lasting two hours, held biweekly from 20 to 34 weeks of pregnancy. The sessions covered topics such as physical and mental changes during pregnancy, common complications, warning signs, nutrition, exercise, labor education, non-pharmacological pain relief methods, and the partner's role during labor. Practical training in breathing, relaxation, massage, and exercises was included. Groups consisted of 10-15 participants. 2. Psychosocial Couple-Based Prevention Programs: Feinberg et al. (2015): This program included nine classes, with four sessions during pregnancy and four postpartum. The focus was on emotional self-management, conflict resolution, communication, and joint parenting strategies. Classes were led by a male-female facilitator team, with the female being a childbirth educator. 3. Telephone-Based Psycho-Education: Fenwick et al. (2015): Two one-hour sessions were conducted at 24 and 34 weeks of gestation. Midwife-led counseling aimed to help women express feelings, address childbirth-related distress, and develop coping strategies. This intervention reduced emotional distress and facilitated recovery. 4. Pelvic Floor Muscle Training (PFMT): Wang et al. (2014): Women were educated on pelvic anatomy, muscle function, and exercises to strengthen pelvic floor muscles. Training included contracting and relaxing muscles for three seconds, followed by rapid contractions. Exercises were performed 2-3 times daily or 150-200 times per day. Follow-up was conducted via telephone every two weeks until six weeks postpartum. 5. Childbirth Training Workshops: Valiani et al. (2014): Workshops were held in three four-hour weekly sessions for groups of 30 participants. Topics included communication, parental roles, delivery methods, pain relief techniques, and postpartum care. Methods such as lectures, role play, and problem-solving were used. 6. Psycho-Educational Group Therapy: Rouhe et al. (2013): Led by psychologists, this therapy included six sessions during pregnancy and one postpartum. Sessions focused on fear and anxiety, labor stages, hospital routines, and parenthood. Relaxation exercises were incorporated, and participants discussed delivery experiences postpartum. 7. Husband Education Programs: Sharifirad et al. (2013): Husbands attended 90-minute sessions covering delivery mechanisms, advantages, and disadvantages of vaginal and cesarean deliveries. Educational tools included lectures, slides, and pamphlets. 8. Natural Childbirth Preparation: Bergström et al. (2009): Four two-hour sessions during pregnancy and one postpartum session focused on non-pharmacological pain relief methods and the partner's role. Practical training in breathing, relaxation, and massage techniques was emphasized. 9. Applied Relaxation Training: Bastani et al. (2006): A nurse-led program based on progressive muscle relaxation and breathing techniques was conducted over seven weekly 90-minute sessions. Participants practiced relaxation techniques at home and maintained daily records. 10. Decision-Aid Booklets: Shorten et al. (2005): Booklets provided evidence-based information on delivery options, risks, and benefits. Women received these at 28 weeks of gestation to help clarify values and make informed decisions. 11. Computerized Decision Aids: Montgomery et al. (2007): Two computer-based interventions provided information on delivery outcomes and decision analysis. These tools helped women evaluate risks and benefits based on personal values. 12. Education for Healthcare Professionals: Heminki et al. (2008): Public health nurses received additional training to emphasize delivery mode discussions during childbirth classes. Leaflets were distributed to pregnant women, and content was discussed during visits from 32 weeks onward. These interventions aim to empower women, involve their partners, and educate healthcare providers to reduce unnecessary cesarean sections while promoting informed decision-making and positive childbirth experiences.
